tea-workers-phagua.desc: Many tea workers in Habiganj descend from communities brought from central and eastern India in the 19th century, and they have kept their own languages and festivals. Phagua, celebrated around Holi in spring, fills the estates with coloured powder, drumming and group dances. Some estates and community groups now host public gatherings where visitors can watch.
blocks: Good to know
Attend only where welcome; ask before photographing people.

teliapara-tea-estate.desc: In April 1971, senior Bengali officers met at the manager's bungalow of the Teliapara tea estate and laid out the early command structure for the Liberation War. A memorial shaped like a bullet now stands in the garden to mark the meeting. Around it, tea bushes spread across the low hills. It combines naturally with a visit to Satchari.
blocks: How to get there
Near the Dhaka–Sylhet highway close to Satchari, in Madhabpur upazila; reachable by CNG from the highway.
Good to know
Ask the estate for permission before walking into the gardens.

glance: 150 km to Habiganj by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
baniachong-sagar-dighi.desc: Baniachong is often described as one of the largest villages in Asia, a sprawling settlement on the edge of the haor wetlands. Its best-known landmark is Sagar Dighi, a very large old tank linked in folk tradition to Rani Kamala, who is said to have sacrificed herself so the pond would fill. The village also has old zamindar houses and a slow, rural rhythm.
blocks: How to get there
About 30–45 minutes by CNG from Habiganj town.
Good to know
In the rainy season, combine with a boat trip on the surrounding haor.

glance: 150 km to Habiganj by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
bithangal-akhra.desc: Bithangal Akhra is a centuries-old Vaishnava religious centre in Baniachong upazila, set among haor wetlands. It has traditional buildings, old artefacts and resident devotees, and hosts gatherings on religious occasions. In the monsoon the surrounding fields turn into open water, and the boat ride there is a slow, beautiful journey across the haor.
blocks: How to get there
Travel from Habiganj town to Baniachong, then ask locally for a boat (monsoon) or road and footpath route (dry season) to Bithangal.
Good to know
Dress modestly and remove shoes in the temple area. Wear a life jacket on boats.

glance: 150 km to Habiganj by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
mashajan-dighi.desc: About five miles south of Habiganj town lies Mashajan's Dighi, a broad, centuries-old reservoir set in a wide stretch of land. Local history credits it to Syed Goyas Uddin, son of the medieval poet Syed Sultan, in the early 1500s. Sufi families in the region dug such tanks for drinking water and farming. Today it is a calm place of open water and village banks that few outsiders visit.
blocks: How to get there
From Habiganj town take a CNG or auto south toward Mashajan (about 30 minutes).
Good to know
Go in the late afternoon for the light on the water. Combine it with the Shankarpasha mosque.

rema-kalenga-wildlife-sanctuary.desc: Rema-Kalenga stretches along the Tripura border in Chunarughat and is among the biggest remaining tracts of natural hill forest in Bangladesh. Trails lead through dense woodland, with chances to see langurs, macaques, squirrels and a large variety of birds. It is less visited than Lawachara and feels wilder.
blocks: How to get there
From Chunarughat or Srimangal, take a jeep or CNG to Kalenga; roads are rough in places.
Good to know
Stay on trails with a local guide; the border is close. Simple local accommodation is available nearby.

glance: 150 km to Habiganj by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
shankarpasha-shahi-mosque.desc: The Shankarpasha mosque at Uchail, south of Habiganj town, dates from the reign of Sultan Alauddin Husain Shah, around 1494–1513 by different readings of its history. Tradition links it to the conquest of Taraf by saints who came in Shah Jalal's wake, and the tomb of Shah Majlis Amin lies beside it. The square brick prayer hall carries one large dome, with three smaller domes over the narrow verandah and thick walls pierced by many doors and windows. It was long swallowed by jungle and has only been rediscovered in recent times, which keeps it off most itineraries.
blocks: How to get there
From Habiganj town take a CNG toward Rajiura union and Uchail village (Habiganj Sadar upazila).
Good to know
It is a working mosque; dress modestly and ask before photographing inside. The pond behind it is a nice spot to sit.

glance: 150 km to Habiganj by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
satchari-national-park.desc: Satchari, meaning 'seven streams', is a protected forest surrounded by tea estates in Chunarughat. Short and long trails wind beneath tall trees, crossing sandy stream beds. Hoolock gibbons, Phayre's and capped langurs, and many birds live here, and a canopy watchtower helps with sightings. A Tripura village sits within the park area.
blocks: How to get there
On the Dhaka–Sylhet highway; buses can drop you at the park gate, about 1 hour from Habiganj town.
Good to know
Go early, walk quietly, and hire a guide for the longer trail. Wear leech socks in the rains.

glance: Old sweet shops in Habiganj town, such as Adi Gopal
habiganj-rosogolla.desc: Habiganj town has several old sweet shops whose rosogolla and roshmalai are well regarded locally, with shops such as Adi Gopal known by name. The rosogolla here are soft and springy, soaked in a light syrup. A box makes a good gift on the way through.

glance: Rice hotels in Habiganj town and Baniachong bazar
habiganj-haor-fish.desc: The haors of western Habiganj are among the most productive freshwater fisheries in the country. Markets in Baniachong and Habiganj fill with fish such as boal, rui, koi and many small native species, especially as the water recedes after the monsoon. Local cooks make light curries with potato or vegetables, and crispy fried small fish.
